newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Father says N.Korean defectors carried poison.
newsitem.headline: Father says N.Korean defectors carried poison.

text.p: The 79-year-old Korean exile who helped his daughter and her 16-member family stage North Korea's biggest defection has revealed the escapees carried poison to take in case of capture.

In a chilling account of how far the band was prepared to go to flee famine and persecution in Stalinist North Korea, Choi Young-do told South Korean reporters in New York that four years ago he started searching for the daughter he had not seen in 50 years.
Choi's account was published in Seoul newspapers on Tuesday, a day after the 17 defectors arrived from Hong Kong to take up asylum in South Korea.

The flight involved a 27-day trek down the length of China where the band, including young children, posed as travelling rural labourers, pretending even to work in fields to avoid the suspicion of Chinese police.

"The family was prepared for the possibility of arrest by Chinese law enforcement authorities after their escape, as all of them were carrying poison to commit suicide if need be," Choi said at a restaurant in New York where he has lived since emigrating from Seoul.

Choi's eldest daughter, Choi Hyon-sil, 57, her husband, their five sons and daughters, one seven-months pregnant, their wives and husbands, five grandchildren, and a border guard cousin made the escape across the frozen Tuman river into China on October 26.
On November 23, they were smuggled into Hong Kong and on Monday were flown to a new life in South Korea.
"I was in agony from the time that my daughter and her family fled from North Korea to when they safely arrived in South Korea," Choi said. "I was so unsettled."

In a story typical of the way families were torn apart on the Korean Peninsula at the end of World War Two and during the bitter 1950-53 Korean War, Choi said he and his wife last saw their daughter 50 years ago when she was just seven.
Separated from their daughter during confusion at the end of World War Two, the couple made their way from their home in now North Korea to South Korea.
They moved to the United States in the mid-1970s.
Four years ago they determined to find their daughter, described by South Korean media as the "matriarch" of the family of defectors.
"I first started by asking about her whereabouts, then communicated with her by letters and began sending her an allowance," Choi said.
Worried by reports of famine in North Korea, Choi said he started to plan the escape seriously earlier this year.
His wife visited China and in a secret meeting with their daughter who briefly slipped out of North Korea to see her mother, the plan for the escape was worked out.
While in China, Choi's wife also made contacts with some of the two million ethnic Koreans living there. They acted as guides and provided safe houses for the group on their flight.
Choi estimated the escape cost him only "several tens of thousands of dollars."
"Please understand that the exact details of the escape money and people who helped in the escape cannot be revealed," he said.
South Korean officials said the defectors ate a light breakfast on their first full day in their new home and then had medical tests which showed they were all healthy.
The officials said the group was likely to meet the press on December 18 when all their debriefings were finished.
